name: Sara Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and answer parcel-return calls and chats at the contact centre. I finished secondary school and have been on the desk only a short time; I still get mixed up when a returned parcel shows on two screens. The wage is low. A coworker showed me the approved AI summary, which I use now and then, but I check the parcel number before I repeat it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mei prepares meals at a community kitchen, and our children are grown and living independently. We have less than a month of expenses saved, and only a few other centres are near us. I may be closer to retirement than the younger agents, but I have not worked out a date I can afford. I like the calls where I find the parcel and the customer can stop worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my desk AI Plateau sounds like a tidier summary, not a person finding a missing parcel. I would still check the tracking number myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my shifts would stay, but low pay and less than a month saved make me nervous before any new tool arrives. Mei’s kitchen pay varies with the number of meals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep answering returns calls and compare the occasional AI summary with the tracking page before sending it. In the first year of this small change, I’d stop buying coffee on my two early shifts and keep the money for travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about bills, comfortable with a little help on the screen. A parcel can be found later; a bus fare has to be paid before the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the AI note get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Friday the AI note said a package had reached the depot. The tracking page said it had only left the sender, so I corrected the reply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei (my partner) would pack a flask for those early shifts. We have not promised ourselves a new savings target; the first job is to keep getting to work.

say: I’d tell agents to **check tracking numbers** against summaries.
I’d say **returns calls** still need a person in this mild picture.
think: I think my **shifts continue** with only small AI shortcuts.
I worry **thin savings** and low pay leave little room for a missed week.
do: Keep **answering returns calls** and verify occasional AI summaries against tracking.
Stop buying **early-shift coffee** twice weekly and keep the cost for travel.
feel: **Anxious** about bills, comfortable with small tool help.
S0.quote: A parcel can be found later; a bus fare has to be paid before the shift.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** includes checking the original tracking page.
The **low wage** makes travel money a present concern.
Coffee cuts protect **work transport**, not a new investment plan.

steps.text: Keep taking returns calls and verify occasional AI summaries against tracking pages
Skip coffee on two early shifts and hold its cost for bus travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could answer the easy “where is my parcel” chats before I have learned the difficult ones. I would ask for the paid rota and time to correct wrong tracking replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can pick up a proven screen, but the centre may cut the junior shifts first. We have few local alternatives and Mei’s kitchen wage will not cover both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d learn the new AI exception view by checking fifteen old returns with Rosa on a paid shift. In the first year routine parcel chats move, I’d apply for posted paid returns work nearby only if its written weekly wage and hours cover our bills after travel; I would keep my current job until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing shifts, willing to try the screen. I can test fifteen cases without betting our rent on the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which exception would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would include a return that the AI called delivered even though it was still at the depot. Rosa can show me the evidence tab, then I can check it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make another rota workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei (my partner) starts kitchen work early. I would compare the first bus and full pay week before accepting another centre’s rota.

say: I’d ask for **paid junior hours** as easy chats move.
I’d show **wrong tracking replies** from tested old returns.
think: I think I can learn a **proven exception screen**.
I fear **junior shift cuts** with few nearby job options.
do: Learn **AI exception view** through fifteen old returns with Rosa on paid time.
Seek **posted paid returns work** with written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours and bus access; keep current job until signing.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, willing to test a tool.
S1.quote: I can test fifteen cases without betting our rent on the tool.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** is a specific paid-shift test, unlike occasional summaries.
A second centre must fit **first-bus times** and whole-week pay.
Her manager inquiry is **individual**, not collective action.

steps.text: Learn new AI exception view using fifteen old returns with Rosa on paid time
Apply for posted returns with written after-fare bill-covering wages/hours and reachable first bus
Keep current paid returns job until a suitable offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 could trace parcels and answer customers without us. Robots around 2031 come later, but my current work is on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might lose the junior rota while I am still learning it. Less than a month saved means Mei and I would notice the first missing pay at the next bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d ask management for written cut dates and inspect posted paid counter jobs on the early bus route. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I’d move only on a signed offer showing written weekly pay and hours that cover bills after travel; I would stay at the centre until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. A new job has to start with a wage, not a hopeful interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the counter manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the counter manager whether there is a paid vacancy and what time the first shift begins. A bus that arrives late would cost me the job before I learned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could family help with travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could ask our grown daughter Lila whether she can drive me for one week if a first shift starts before the bus, but she has her own job. I would not promise an employer she can do it unless she agrees.

say: I’d ask for **written cut dates** on returns calls.
I’d say **2028 AGI** reaches parcel screens before robots.
think: I think my **junior rota** could disappear soon.
I know **under one month saved** cannot bridge a long job search.
do: Request **written cut dates** and inspect posted counter jobs on the early bus route.
Move after calls end only on **signed after-travel bill-covering pay**, written hours and a reachable shift.
Ask **daughter Lila** about one week of rides only if the first shift starts before buses; do not assume agreement.
S2.quote: A new job has to start with a wage, not a hopeful interview.
fieldNote: Her **screen job** faces AGI in 2028, before robots.
Lila’s rides are **uncertain and bounded** to one week.
A signed counter offer needs **reachable shifts** and after-travel bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Inspect posted paid counter vacancies reachable by early bus
Move after calls end on signed written after-travel bill-covering weekly wages/hours with reachable shift
Ask Lila for one week of rides only if first shift precedes buses and she agrees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives me time to practise a different counter job while I still have paid hours. I would ask to see a real posted vacancy before anyone sells me a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could handle the local library’s returns desk if a patient worker showed me the records. Full thinking AI could still catalogue returns, so I need to know which work remains paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d request a supervised paid trial at the library returns desk only if it posts a paid opening. If that role requires a records course, I’d take it only with employer-funded fees and paid study hours. In the first year after 2031 I’d move only with a signed offer showing weekly wages and hours that cover bills after bus fare, keeping my current shift until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with time to test a desk before leaving. A library badge is not the same as a paid week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would follow one returned book from the drop box to the borrower record with somebody watching. If the job is mostly a computer moving entries, I would keep looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mei compare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mei (my partner) and I would check the library’s weekend rota against the bus schedule. The extra journey cannot swallow the wage difference.

say: I’d ask for a **posted paid library opening** before studying.
I’d request a **supervised paid trial** on real returns.
think: I think I could learn **library records** with patient help.
I know **2031 AGI** could catalogue books too.
do: Try **supervised paid library work** only for a posted paid opening; reject roles mostly shifting computer entries.
Take a **required records course** only for that posted paid library role with employer-funded fees and paid study hours.
Move after 2031 to **posted paid library work** on signed weekly bill-covering wages/hours after bus fare, with reachable weekend buses.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to try paid work.
S3.quote: A library badge is not the same as a paid week.
fieldNote: The **library trial** must be paid and tied to a posted opening.
A required course needs **funded study** and paid work time.
A reachable **weekend bus** and full weekly pay govern the move.

steps.text: Try supervised paid library shift only for posted paid opening
Take required records course only for posted paid library role with employer-funded fees and study hours
Move only on signed after-fare bill-covering weekly wages, hours and weekend bus access
Reject library roles mostly shifting entries by computer and continue searching

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to watch paid hours, not a guarantee that everyone my age will stop working. I would ask management for the junior rota each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still need my wage at 68; I have not checked what retirement income Mei and I would actually have. Full thinking AI could still take parcel calls in 2036, and robots around 2039 are later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep taking paid parcel calls and record the wage, bills and savings before choosing any retirement date. In the first year after 2036, if I still need wages and call hours fall, I’d move to a posted paid desk job only on a signed offer showing weekly wages and hours covering bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, even with more time. Ten years can pass quickly when you are waiting for savings to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose a stop date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check actual income and savings with Mei before I chose a date to stop. I would not put a pension amount on the page until I had seen proof of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would grown children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own bills. I would not write either of their wages into our retirement plan without an offer from them.

say: I’d request the **yearly junior rota** while calls remain.
I’d say **older agents** may still need wages after 2036.
think: I think I may **need wages at 68** if retirement income falls short.
I cannot assume **pension income** I have not verified.
do: Keep **paid parcel calls** and compare actual wages, bills and savings in 2026.
Move if wages remain needed after cuts to **posted paid desk work**, on signed weekly wages/hours covering bills after travel.
S4.quote: I would not put a pension amount on the page until I had seen proof of it.
fieldNote: She treats **retirement income** as unknown until checked.
Her **thin cushion** remains a present worry despite ten years.
Grown children’s **help is unpromised**, not budgeted income.

steps.text: Keep taking paid parcel calls and compare actual wages, bills and savings
Move if wages remain needed after cuts to posted paid desks with signed after-travel bill-covering wages/hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could trace a parcel more quickly than I can while I am still learning the job, and our thin savings would not carry a long gap. I would need notice of paid-hour cuts and a real posted opening with enough weekly pay after travel.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the new job is reachable at the time it starts. A vacancy on the last bus route can disappear when the first shift begins before the buses run.

headlineQuote: A vacancy on the last bus route can disappear when the first shift begins before the buses run.
portrait: At **58**, Sara is a junior returns agent still learning after secondary school.
She and Mei have **grown children**, low household reserves and less than one month saved.
She earns **lower pay** and sees only a few similar centres nearby.
She uses **AI occasionally**, checking parcel numbers against original records.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could take the parcel tracing she is still learning before another wage appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid-hour notice** and a real reachable job with enough after-travel weekly pay would help.
